newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: AUSTRALIA GOLD-EXPORT UNDER THREAT FROM PRICE FALL.
newsitem.headline: AUSTRALIA GOLD-EXPORT UNDER THREAT FROM PRICE FALL.

text.p: Australian gold miners have told the government that exports of gold from Australia may fall short of a forecast 356 tonnes in 1997/98.
Australia exports about 90 percent of the gold it mines, generating A$5.6 billion in 1995/96, and re-exports Pacific Islands gold refined in Australia,

"In 1997/98, Australian exports of gold were forecast to increase by 6.3 percent to over 356 tonnes, reflecting strong growth in domestic production," the Association of Mining and Exploration Companies (AMEC) of Australia said.

"However, AMEC believes there are serious doubts as to whether this forecast can now be achieved given the recent dramatic fall in world gold prices, threatening the viability of many marginal mines and causing an upwards readjustment of mine cut-off grades," AMEC said in a submission to the government.
The submission was made late last month in the wake of the Australian central bank's sale of 167 tonnes of bullion reserves between January and June, which was kept secret until July 4.
The news temporarily pushed gold down to its lowest price in 12 years, prompting fears among miners that higher cost deposits would become marginal.
"Gold miners have found it difficult to deal with the fall in the gold price and other factors such as high costs and royalties," said AMEC executive officer of economics Adrienne Wright.
Miners have criticised the government for selling the reserves, but senior government officials refuse to accept blame for the effect on local and international markets.
Reserve Bank governor Ian Macfarlane told executives at a business dinner in Perth on Wednesday that the mining industry had exaggerated the impact of the sales.
He noted that gold was only about US$6 an ounce higher on July 4 than the current price of around US$326 an ounce.
Last month deputy prime minister Tim Fischer laid the blame on "24-year-old screen jockeys."
Whoever is to blame, it is clear the mining industry is smarting under current conditions.

Analysts estimate that 26 percent of the gold produced in Australia carries cash costs in excess of A$430 an ounce. On top of cash costs miners must factor in amortisation , depreciation and other expenses. Gold currently returns about A$440 an ounce.
That Australian gold miners are among the most active in the world in pre-selling their future gold production at higher prices through hedging should come as no surprise.
The costs among Australian producers on average are among the highest, if not the highest in the world.

While the Australian sale of 167 tonnes of gold bullion generated A$2.4 billion in income, AMEC estimates that Australia could lose at least A$1 billion in export earnings over the next year as a direct result of the fallout from the sales.
